```{r knitr-setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 110)
```

# Data Analysis Template (R, beginner version)

**Contents** (the big sections)

0. Packages and settings
1. Load `raw`
2. Missing values
3. Variable selection (forward / backward, AIC / BIC)
4. Check the assumptions of the selected lm
5. Transformations: Box-Cox for y, and a light try for the x
6. Outliers (and how they differ from the normal rows)
7. Interactions
8. The models, fitted on all of `raw`, and their plots
9. Model comparison: moving window (train = the last 60 days)
10. The holdout (once)

**Part B. Classification** (the TARGET is a category): sections B-0 ... B-10, at the end of this file.

- **This file has two parts: Part A (the TARGET is a number) and Part B (the TARGET is a category, at the end).** Run Part A **or** Part B, not both: they use the same names (`TARGET`, `raw`, `dat` ...). Part B has its own settings and starts from the same files of the EDA template.
- This template reads the files written by the EDA template (`raw.rds`, `roles.rds`, and at the very end `holdout.rds`).
- **You decide the analysis.** The template runs the steps and shows the numbers; the places where **you decide** are marked `# <-- YOUR DECISION`:
  `SELECTED` (section 3), `X_TRANS` (section 5), `OUTLIER_COL` (section 6), `COLUMN1` / `COLUMN2` / `INTER_ADD` (section 7).
- The order of the steps: variable selection with lm -> check the lm -> transform y once with Box-Cox (and maybe a few x) -> look at the outliers -> interactions -> fit the models -> compare them with a moving window -> the holdout. **Box-Cox is done once and never again.**
- **Time series is the default:** the models are always trained on the **last `WINDOW` days** before the days they predict (default 60), and moved forward by `TEST_DAYS` days (default 7). Without a time column (`TIME <- NULL`) K-fold is used instead.

**What to change for a new data set (and where it is)**

| what | where |
|---|---|
| `TARGET`, `TIME` (`NULL` = no time column), `GROUP` (`NULL` = none) | chunk `settings` (section 0): the three required settings |
| the length of the moving window, the number of days predicted at once, the family of the glm | `settings`: `WINDOW`, `TEST_DAYS`, `GLM_FAMILY` |
| the numeric / categorical predictors | the EDA template wrote them to `roles.rds`. To use your own lists, write `NUM <- c(...)` and `CAT <- c(...)` in chunk `load-raw` |
| y has zeros | `settings`: `Y_SHIFT <- 1` (then `log(y + 1)` is used if Box-Cox says log) |
| which variable-selection result | section 3, chunk `select-final`: `SELECTED` |
| which transformations of the x | section 5, chunk `x-trans`: `X_TRANS` |
| which column is checked for outliers, and the rule | section 6, chunk `outlier-check`: `OUTLIER_COL`, `K_IQR`, `OUTLIER_BY` |
| which interactions | section 7: option 1 = chunk `inter-test` (`COLUMN1`, `COLUMN2`, then `inter-add`), option 2 = chunks `inter-scan` and `inter-scan-add` (`INTER_ADD`). Both fill `INTER_SEL` |

### Notation (the same in the EDA template)

| name | meaning |
|---|---|
| `raw` | the rows we explore, select variables on, and compare the models on |
| `holdout` | the last rows (days), opened **once** at the end (section 10) |
| `dat` | `raw` with the missing values filled (section 2): used in sections 3-8 |
| `full` | `raw` followed by `holdout` (section 10) |
| `NUM`, `CAT` | the numeric and the categorical predictors |

# Part A. Regression (the TARGET is a number)

## 0. Packages and settings

```{r settings}
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "glmnet", "lme4", "MASS", "car"))     # run once if a package is missing
library(tidyverse)
options(width = 150)

# ===== Settings =====
SEED       <- 0
TARGET     <- "realized_vol"            # the numeric outcome (y)
TIME       <- "date"               # the time column. NULL if the data has no time column
GROUP      <- "ticker"         # a column whose values repeat (the same station / customer ...). NULL if none

WINDOW     <- 180                   # moving window: the models are trained on the last 60 days before the days they predict
TEST_DAYS  <- 30                    # ... and predict the next 7 days, then the window moves forward by 7 days
FOLDS      <- 5                    # K-fold (only used when there is no time column)

GLM_FAMILY <- Gamma(link = "log")  # glm / glmm for a positive outcome that is skewed. Counts: poisson(link = "log").  Other: gaussian()
Y_SHIFT    <- 0                    # if y has zeros: 1  (Box-Cox needs y > 0; then log(y + 1) is used)
# ====================

HAS_TIME <- !is.null(TIME)
set.seed(SEED)
```

## 1. Load `raw`

```{r load-raw}
raw   <- readRDS("raw.rds")         # written by the EDA template (section 11-4)
roles <- readRDS("roles.rds")
NUM   <- roles$NUM                  # numeric predictors   (your own list: NUM <- c("temp_c", "rain_mm"))
CAT   <- roles$CAT                  # categorical predictors (your own list: CAT <- c("station_type"))

if (HAS_TIME) {
  raw <- raw[order(raw[[TIME]]), ]
  raw$.day <- as.Date(raw[[TIME]])  # the day of every row (the moving window works with days)
}
stopifnot(all(c(TARGET, NUM, CAT, GROUP) %in% names(raw)))

cat("raw:", nrow(raw), "rows | numeric predictors:", length(NUM), "| categorical predictors:", length(CAT), "\n")
NUM
CAT
CAT <- CAT[CAT != "sector"]
full$sector = NULL

```

## 2. Prepare `dat`

There is **nothing to decide here: just run the chunk.** It makes two things:

- `dat`: `raw` with the categorical columns turned into factors (the form the models need). The missing values of the predictors were already filled in the EDA template (its section 11), so there is normally nothing left to fill. Sections 3-8 use `dat`.
- `fill_missing(train, test)`: used again inside every model of sections 8-10, just before the model is fitted. It makes the categories the same in train and test (a category that is not in train becomes the filler). It is also a **safety net**: a predictor value that is still missing is filled with the **mean of the training rows** (a categorical column: the new category `"Missing"`, or the most frequent category if there was no missing value in the training rows).

The outcome (`TARGET`) is never filled.

```{r fill-missing}
most_common <- function(x) names(sort(table(x), decreasing = TRUE))[1]

fill_missing <- function(train, test) {
  for (col in NUM) {
    m <- mean(train[[col]], na.rm = TRUE)                 # the mean of the TRAIN rows
    train[[col]][is.na(train[[col]])] <- m
    test[[col]][is.na(test[[col]])]   <- m
  }
  for (col in CAT) {
    train[[col]] <- as.character(train[[col]])
    test[[col]]  <- as.character(test[[col]])
    fill <- if (any(is.na(train[[col]]))) "Missing" else most_common(train[[col]])
    train[[col]][is.na(train[[col]])] <- fill
    test[[col]][is.na(test[[col]]) | !(test[[col]] %in% train[[col]])] <- fill    # NA, or a category that is not in train
    train[[col]] <- factor(train[[col]])
    test[[col]]  <- factor(test[[col]], levels = levels(train[[col]]))             # the same levels in train and test
  }
  list(train = train, test = test)
}

dat <- fill_missing(raw, raw)$train                       # raw with factors (and anything that is still missing filled)

# check: nothing should be missing in the predictors (0 = the EDA template did its job)
cat("missing values in the predictors: raw", sum(is.na(raw[c(NUM, CAT)])), "| dat", sum(is.na(dat[c(NUM, CAT)])), "\n")
```

## 3. Variable selection (forward / backward, AIC / BIC)

Four ways to select the variables of an lm:

- **forward**: start from no variable and add the variable that helps most, until nothing helps;
- **backward**: start from all variables and remove the one that hurts least, until every one is needed;
- **AIC** keeps more variables, **BIC** keeps fewer (a bigger penalty for every variable).

```{r select-four}
m_null <- lm(reformulate("1", TARGET), data = dat)
m_full <- lm(reformulate(c(NUM, CAT), TARGET), data = dat)
n      <- nrow(dat)

sel <- list(
  forward_AIC  = step(m_null, scope = formula(m_full), direction = "forward",  trace = 0),
  forward_BIC  = step(m_null, scope = formula(m_full), direction = "forward",  trace = 0, k = log(n)),
  backward_AIC = step(m_full, direction = "backward", trace = 0),
  backward_BIC = step(m_full, direction = "backward", trace = 0, k = log(n)))
sel$full <- m_full

# the four results and the full model side by side
data.frame(n_terms = sapply(sel, function(m) length(attr(terms(m), "term.labels"))),
           AIC     = round(sapply(sel, AIC), 1),
           BIC     = round(sapply(sel, BIC), 1),
           adj_R2  = round(sapply(sel, function(m) summary(m)$adj.r.squared), 4))

for (nm in names(sel)) cat(nm, ":", attr(terms(sel[[nm]]), "term.labels"), "\n\n")
```

```{r select-final}
SELECTED <- "forward_AIC"      # <-- YOUR DECISION: "forward_AIC" | "forward_BIC" | "backward_AIC" | "backward_BIC" | "full"

formula_sel <- formula(sel[[SELECTED]])                  # the selected formula: everything below is built on it
sel_terms   <- attr(terms(formula_sel), "term.labels")   # its terms
formula_sel
```

## 4. Check the assumptions of the selected lm

```{r assumptions}
ols <- lm(formula_sel, data = dat)

# 1 Residuals vs Fitted : the points should scatter evenly around 0 (a curve = the shape is wrong; a funnel = the spread grows)
# 2 Normal Q-Q          : the points should lie on the line (the residuals are normal)
# 3 Scale-Location      : the red line should be flat (the spread is constant)
# 4 Cook's distance     : a few very tall bars are rows that pull the fit
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(ols, which = 1:4)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

hist(resid(ols), main = "Residuals", xlab = "residual")                       # should look like a bell

plot(ols)

if (HAS_TIME) {                                                               # the residuals should not drift or wave over time
  plot(dat$.day, resid(ols), main = "Residuals over time", xlab = "day", ylab = "residual")
  abline(h = 0, col = "red")
}

# Variance inflation factor: larger than 5-10 = the variable is explained by the other variables
tryCatch(car::vif(ols), error = function(e) "VIF cannot be computed: some columns are explained by the others (aliased). Look for two variables with the same information.")
```

## 5. Transformations

### 5-1. Box-Cox: transform y (once)

Box-Cox looks for the power `lambda` that makes the residuals of the lm most normal. The plot shows the best `lambda` and its 95% interval. **The rule here: `LAM` = the nearest integer of `lambda hat`.**

| `LAM` | the transformed y | |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | `y^2` | |
| 1 | `y` | no transformation |
| 0 | `log(y)` | (or `log(y + 1)` when y has zeros: `Y_SHIFT <- 1`) |
| -1 | `1/y` | |

This is done **once**. After it, every model is trained on the transformed y, and the predictions are **turned back** (`from_t()`) before any error is computed.

```{r boxcox}
dat$.y0 <- dat[[TARGET]] + Y_SHIFT
stopifnot("y + Y_SHIFT must be larger than 0: if y has zeros, write Y_SHIFT <- 1 in the settings" = all(dat$.y0 > 0))

bc      <- MASS::boxcox(reformulate(sel_terms, ".y0"), data = dat, lambda = seq(-2, 2, 0.05))
lam_hat <- bc$x[which.max(bc$y)]
LAM     <- as.integer(round(lam_hat))       # <-- YOUR DECISION if you disagree: write LAM <- 1 (no transformation) or another integer
cat("lambda hat =", round(lam_hat, 2), "-> LAM =", LAM, "\n")

to_t   <- function(y) if (LAM == 0) log(y + Y_SHIFT) else if (LAM == 1) y else (y + Y_SHIFT)^LAM              # y -> the transformed y
from_t <- function(z) if (LAM == 0) exp(z) - Y_SHIFT else if (LAM == 1) z else pmax(z, 1e-8)^(1 / LAM) - Y_SHIFT   # the transformed y -> y

dat$.y <- to_t(dat[[TARGET]])
ols_t  <- lm(reformulate(sel_terms, ".y"), data = dat)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))                         # the residuals before and after: the right one should be closer to the line
qqnorm(resid(ols),   main = "Q-Q plot: y");                 qqline(resid(ols))
qqnorm(resid(ols_t), main = paste("Q-Q plot: transformed y (LAM =", LAM, ")")); qqline(resid(ols_t))
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

### 5-2. A light try: transform the numeric x

For every numeric variable of the selected formula: does adding `x^2`, `log(x)`, `sqrt(x)` or `exp(x)` help the lm of the transformed y? A negative `AIC_change` = better. A small `p_value` = the new term is useful.

```{r x-trans}
m_sel  <- lm(reformulate(sel_terms, ".y"), data = dat)
num_in <- intersect(NUM, all.vars(formula_sel))             # the numeric variables of the selected formula

tried <- NULL
for (x in num_in) {
  v <- dat[[x]]
  if (n_distinct(v) <= 2) next                              # a 0/1 variable: nothing to transform
  terms_try <- paste0("I(", x, "^2)")                       # x squared
  if (min(v) > 0)  terms_try <- c(terms_try, paste0("log(", x, ")"))     # only possible for positive x
  if (min(v) >= 0) terms_try <- c(terms_try, paste0("sqrt(", x, ")"))    # only possible for x >= 0
  if (max(v) < 20) terms_try <- c(terms_try, paste0("exp(", x, ")"))     # (a big x makes exp(x) explode)
  for (tt in terms_try) {
    m2 <- lm(reformulate(c(sel_terms, tt), ".y"), data = dat)
    tried <- rbind(tried, data.frame(term = tt, AIC_change = round(AIC(m2) - AIC(m_sel), 1), p_value = round(anova(m_sel, m2)[2, "Pr(>F)"], 4)))
  }
}
if (!is.null(tried)) tried[order(tried$AIC_change), ]

X_TRANS <- character(0)      # <-- YOUR DECISION: the terms you want to add, for example c("I(temp_c^2)", "log(rain_mm + 1)"). character(0) = none
```


## 6. Outliers

Outliers are looked at **only through the target**, with the lm we already have: the selected variables (section 3) + `X_TRANS` (section 5), fitted on the transformed y. A row is an **outlier candidate** if this lm misses its target by a lot:

- **standardized residual** = (actual - predicted) / the typical error, on the transformed y. A row is a candidate if its absolute value is larger than `R_LIMIT` (3 is the usual choice).
- **Cook's distance** = how much one row pulls the lm by itself. It is shown as a column: a big value means the row really changes the fit.

The candidates are collected in the table `out_rows` (the worst first): **look at them** (`View(out_rows)`). Then the chunk shows how they differ from the normal rows, column by column (for example: the mean of `temp_c` is 18 in the normal rows and 22 in the candidates). Nothing is removed from `dat`.

```{r outlier-check}
R_LIMIT <- 3        # <-- CHANGE HERE (optional): a row is an outlier candidate if |standardized residual| is larger than this

# 1. the lm (selected variables + X_TRANS, transformed y) and the numbers of every row
m_out     <- lm(reformulate(c(sel_terms, X_TRANS), ".y"), data = dat, na.action = na.exclude)
dat$.rstd <- rstandard(m_out)                                      # standardized residual
dat$.cook <- cooks.distance(m_out)                                 # Cook's distance
dat$.pred <- from_t(predict(m_out, dat))                           # the lm's prediction, back in the units of y
dat$.out  <- (abs(dat$.rstd) > R_LIMIT) %in% TRUE                  # TRUE = outlier candidate
cat(sum(dat$.out), "outlier candidates in", nrow(dat), "rows (", round(100 * mean(dat$.out), 1), "%)\n")

# 2. the picture: standardized residual of every row (red = candidate)
plot(if (HAS_TIME) dat$.day else seq_len(nrow(dat)), dat$.rstd, pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = ifelse(dat$.out, "red", "grey40"),
     xlab = if (HAS_TIME) "day" else "row", ylab = "standardized residual", main = "Standardized residual (red = outlier candidate)")
abline(h = c(-R_LIMIT, R_LIMIT), lty = 2)

# 3. the candidates, collected (the worst first): LOOK AT THEM
front    <- c(TIME, GROUP, TARGET, ".pred", ".rstd", ".cook")      # the columns to read first
out_rows <- dat[dat$.out, c(front, setdiff(c(NUM, CAT), front))]
out_rows <- out_rows[order(-abs(out_rows$.rstd)), ]
head(out_rows, 20)
# View(out_rows)                                                   # (optional) in RStudio: the whole table

```

```{r outlier-compare}
# 4. numeric columns: the mean in the normal rows and in the outlier candidates
if (any(dat$.out) && any(!dat$.out)) {
  cols <- c(TARGET, NUM)
  cmp  <- data.frame(normal  = sapply(dat[!dat$.out, cols], mean, na.rm = TRUE),
                     outlier = sapply(dat[dat$.out,  cols], mean, na.rm = TRUE))
  cmp$diff_in_sd <- (cmp$outlier - cmp$normal) / sapply(dat[cols], sd, na.rm = TRUE)     # the difference / the overall sd: below 0.2 tiny, above 0.8 large
  print(round(cmp[order(-abs(cmp$diff_in_sd)), ], 2))                                    # the biggest differences first
}

# 5. categories: what share of every category is an outlier candidate? (compare it with the overall share)
if (any(dat$.out)) {
  cat("\nthe overall share of candidates:", round(100 * mean(dat$.out), 1), "%\n")
  share <- do.call(rbind, lapply(unique(c(CAT, GROUP)), function(v) {
    g     <- as.character(dat[[v]]);  g[is.na(g)] <- "NA"
    n_all <- tapply(dat$.out, g, length)
    n_out <- tapply(dat$.out, g, sum)
    data.frame(column = v, category = names(n_all), n = as.vector(n_all), n_outlier = as.vector(n_out),
               pct = round(100 * as.vector(n_out) / as.vector(n_all), 1))
  }))
  share <- share[share$n >= 5, ]                                                         # tiny categories are left out
  print(head(share[order(-share$pct), ], 15), row.names = FALSE)                         # the 15 categories with the highest share
  if (HAS_TIME) print(round(100 * tapply(dat$.out, format(dat$.day, "%Y-%m"), mean), 1)) # the share in every month
}
```

**How to read the result**

- Look at `out_rows` first: are the candidates one station, one period, one kind of day? Is the actual target far above (or below) `.pred`?
- Numeric columns: a large `diff_in_sd` means the candidates live in a different part of that column (for example hotter days). Categories: a `pct` much larger than the overall share means the candidates are concentrated there.
- **A clear pattern** = the lm misses something that this column explains. Keep the rows and give the model that information: the variable (section 3), a transformation (section 5) or an **interaction** (next section).
- **No pattern**: the candidates look random (a data error? a one-off event?). Check the rows by hand before you decide what to do.


## 7. Interactions

An interaction `a:b` means: the effect of `a` is different for different values of `b`. There are **two options**, and both fill the same list `INTER_SEL` (the interactions you keep). Use one of them, or both, as many times as you like. (Outliers that are explained by two variables together, section 6, are a good reason to test that pair.)

- **OPTION 1: you choose the pair.** Write `COLUMN1` and `COLUMN2` (any two columns of `dat`, numeric or categorical), run the test, **look at the result, and decide**: run the chunk `inter-add` to add the pair, or skip it. Then go back to `COLUMN1` / `COLUMN2` and test the next pair.
- **OPTION 2: scan.** The variables of the selected formula are tried in pairs, **one interaction at a time**, and the table shows the pairs with the smallest p-value. You write the ones you want in `INTER_ADD`.

With many pairs (option 2) a few small p-values come by chance: prefer the very small ones that also make sense.

```{r inter-start}
# Run this chunk ONCE (it empties INTER_SEL): do NOT run it again after you have added interactions.
RHS       <- c(sel_terms, X_TRANS)                                          # the terms until now
INTER_SEL <- character(0)                                                   # the interactions kept (OPTION 1 and OPTION 2 add to it)
RHS_FINAL <- unique(c(RHS, unlist(strsplit(INTER_SEL, ":")), INTER_SEL))    # THE FORMULA FROM NOW ON (an interaction brings the main effects of its two columns)
```

### OPTION 1: test the pair you choose

The chunks of option 1 name specific columns (`temp_c`, `station_type` ...), so they are `eval = FALSE`: **they are not run when you knit**. Write your own columns and run them by hand.

```{r inter-test, eval=FALSE}
# ===== The pair to test: CHANGE HERE, then run this chunk =====
COLUMN1 <- "temp_c"            # <-- CHANGE HERE: any column (numeric or categorical)
COLUMN2 <- "station_type"      # <-- CHANGE HERE: another column (numeric or categorical)
# ==============================================================

stopifnot("COLUMN1 and COLUMN2 must be two different columns" = COLUMN1 != COLUMN2,
          "COLUMN1 and COLUMN2 must be columns of dat"        = all(c(COLUMN1, COLUMN2) %in% names(dat)))
INTER_TEST <- paste(COLUMN1, COLUMN2, sep = ":")                            # "a:b"
same_inter <- c(INTER_TEST, paste(COLUMN2, COLUMN1, sep = ":"))             # "a:b" and "b:a" are the same interaction
inter_keep <- setdiff(INTER_SEL, same_inter)                                # the interactions kept before (without this one: it is the one tested)
base_terms <- unique(c(RHS, COLUMN1, COLUMN2, unlist(strsplit(inter_keep, ":")), inter_keep))   # the model WITHOUT this interaction (the main effects of both columns are in)

# A column that never changes inside a group (a station's capacity ...): the interaction of TWO such columns only builds the group ID again
if (!is.null(GROUP) && all(sapply(c(COLUMN1, COLUMN2), function(v) all(tapply(dat[[v]], dat[[GROUP]], n_distinct) == 1)))) {
  cat("WARNING: both columns never change inside a", GROUP, ": the p-value is meaningless\n")
}

# F-test in the lm of the transformed y: a small p-value = the interaction helps
lm0  <- lm(reformulate(base_terms, ".y"),                data = dat)
lm1  <- lm(reformulate(c(base_terms, INTER_TEST), ".y"), data = dat)
a_lm <- anova(lm0, lm1)
a_lm
cat("\n", INTER_TEST, ": p-value =", signif(a_lm[2, "Pr(>F)"], 3), "  -> add it? run the chunk inter-add (or skip it)\n")
```

#### (optional) The same pair in a glm and in a mixed model

The **same** pair (`COLUMN1`, `COLUMN2`) with the other model types (likelihood-ratio test), to help you decide. It only shows the numbers.

```{r inter-other, eval=FALSE}
# glm (the original y): a small p-value = the interaction helps
anova(glm(reformulate(base_terms, TARGET),                  family = GLM_FAMILY, data = dat),
      glm(reformulate(c(base_terms, INTER_TEST), TARGET),   family = GLM_FAMILY, data = dat), test = "Chisq")

# mixed model (the transformed y, a random intercept per group)
if (!is.null(GROUP)) {
  re <- paste0("(1 | ", GROUP, ")")
  m0 <- lme4::lmer(reformulate(c(base_terms, re), ".y"),               dat, REML = FALSE)
  m1 <- lme4::lmer(reformulate(c(base_terms, INTER_TEST, re), ".y"),   dat, REML = FALSE)
  anova(m0, m1)
}
```

#### Add the pair (only if you want it)

```{r inter-add, eval=FALSE}
# Run this chunk ONLY if you want the pair of the LAST run of inter-test (INTER_TEST). To leave the pair out: do not run it.
INTER_SEL <- unique(c(setdiff(INTER_SEL, same_inter), INTER_TEST))              # (the same pair in the other order is replaced, not repeated)
RHS_FINAL <- unique(c(RHS, unlist(strsplit(INTER_SEL, ":")), INTER_SEL))        # THE FORMULA FROM NOW ON
# To take one out later:  INTER_SEL <- setdiff(INTER_SEL, "a:b")   and run the RHS_FINAL line again

INTER_SEL          # the interactions kept so far
RHS_FINAL          # the formula from now on
```

### OPTION 2: scan the pairs of the selected variables

```{r inter-scan}
# Which variables are tried in pairs?  FALSE: the variables of the selected formula.  TRUE: ALL the variables of NUM and CAT.
# (A variable can matter only through an interaction, for example "weekend" that helps in one kind of place and hurts in another:
#  its own effect cancels out, so section 3 may have dropped it. TRUE finds such a variable.)
SCAN_ALL <- FALSE
vars   <- if (SCAN_ALL) c(NUM, CAT) else all.vars(formula_sel)[-1]
m_base <- lm(reformulate(unique(c(RHS, vars)), ".y"), data = dat)       # the model with the main effects of all these variables

# A variable that never changes inside a group (a station's capacity ...) can only separate the groups. The interaction of TWO such variables
# only builds the group ID again (the group effect of section 8 does that already, and the p-value is meaningless): leave those pairs out.
group_level <- setNames(rep(FALSE, length(vars)), vars)
if (!is.null(GROUP)) group_level <- sapply(vars, function(v) all(tapply(dat[[v]], dat[[GROUP]], n_distinct) == 1))

pair_terms <- NULL
if (length(vars) >= 2) {
  all_pairs  <- combn(vars, 2, simplify = FALSE)                          # all pairs of variables
  ok_pairs   <- Filter(function(p) !all(group_level[p]), all_pairs)       # without the pairs of two group-level variables
  pair_terms <- sapply(ok_pairs, paste, collapse = ":")                   # "a:b"
}

if (length(pair_terms) > 0) {
  inter_tab <- as.data.frame(add1(m_base, scope = reformulate(c(unique(c(RHS, vars)), pair_terms)), test = "F"))[-1, ]   # [-1, ] removes the row "<none>"
  inter_tab <- inter_tab[order(inter_tab[["Pr(>F)"]]), c("Df", "AIC", "F value", "Pr(>F)")]
  round(head(inter_tab, 15), 4)                                           # the 15 pairs with the smallest p-value
}
```

```{r inter-scan-add}
INTER_ADD <- c("market_cap_bn:vix_prev")    # <-- YOUR DECISION: the interactions of the table above to add, for example c("day_off:station_type"). character(0) = none
INTER_SEL <- c(INTER_SEL, INTER_ADD)
pair_key  <- vapply(strsplit(INTER_SEL, ":"), function(p) paste(sort(p), collapse = ":"), character(1))   # "a:b" and "b:a" are the same interaction
INTER_SEL <- INTER_SEL[!duplicated(pair_key)]                                                            # keep it only once
RHS_FINAL <- unique(c(RHS, unlist(strsplit(INTER_SEL, ":")), INTER_SEL))    # THE FORMULA FROM NOW ON (an interaction brings the main effects of its two variables)

INTER_SEL
RHS_FINAL
ggplot(dat, aes(x = vix_prev, y = realized_vol, color = market_cap_bn) ) + geom_smooth()
```
## 8. The models

### 8-1. The tools (you do not need to change them)

Every model is built from **the same terms** (`RHS_FINAL`). Two functions do everything:

- `fit_model(model, train)` fits a model on the training rows;
- `predict_model(obj, test)` predicts the test rows **in the units of y** (it turns the transformed y back).

| model | what it is | y it is trained on |
|---|---|---|
| `baseline` | the mean of the training y: the number to beat | y |
| `lm` | ordinary least squares | transformed y |
| `lasso` | lm that shrinks the coefficients; some become exactly 0 | transformed y |
| `ridge` | lm that shrinks the coefficients; none becomes 0 | transformed y |
| `glm` | a glm with `GLM_FAMILY` | y |
| `mixed` | lm + a random intercept per `GROUP` | transformed y |
| `glmm` | glm + a random intercept per `GROUP` | y |

A group (station) that is not in the training rows gets the average effect.

```{r tools}
MODELS <- c("baseline", "lm", "lasso", "ridge", "glm", if (!is.null(GROUP)) c("mixed", "glmm"))

# keep only the terms whose variables have at least 2 different values in the training rows
keep_terms <- function(terms, tr) {
  ok <- sapply(terms, function(t) all(sapply(all.vars(parse(text = t)[[1]]), function(v) n_distinct(tr[[v]]) > 1)))
  if (any(ok)) terms[ok] else "1"
}

fit_model <- function(model, tr) {
  terms <- keep_terms(RHS_FINAL, tr)
  tr$.y <- to_t(tr[[TARGET]])                               # the transformed y
  re    <- paste0("(1 | ", GROUP, ")")                      # a random intercept per group
  X     <- function(d) model.matrix(reformulate(terms), d)[, -1, drop = FALSE]    # the numbers for lasso / ridge
  set.seed(SEED)
  fit <- switch(model,
    baseline = mean(tr[[TARGET]]),
    lm       = lm(reformulate(terms, ".y"), data = tr),
    lasso    = glmnet::cv.glmnet(X(tr), tr$.y, alpha = 1),
    ridge    = glmnet::cv.glmnet(X(tr), tr$.y, alpha = 0),
    glm      = glm(reformulate(terms, TARGET), family = GLM_FAMILY, data = tr),
    mixed    = lme4::lmer(reformulate(c(terms, re), ".y"), data = tr, REML = FALSE),
    glmm     = lme4::glmer(reformulate(c(terms, re), TARGET), family = GLM_FAMILY, data = tr))
  list(model = model, fit = fit, terms = terms)
}

predict_model <- function(obj, te) {
  fit <- obj$fit
  switch(obj$model,
    baseline = rep(fit, nrow(te)),
    lm       = from_t(suppressWarnings(predict(fit, te))),
    lasso    = ,
    ridge    = from_t(as.numeric(predict(fit, model.matrix(reformulate(obj$terms), te)[, -1, drop = FALSE], s = "lambda.min"))),
    glm      = as.numeric(predict(fit, te, type = "response")),
    mixed    = from_t(as.numeric(predict(fit, te, allow.new.levels = TRUE))),
    glmm     = as.numeric(predict(fit, te, type = "response", allow.new.levels = TRUE)))
}

# fill the missing values with the TRAIN numbers, fit on train, predict test
fit_predict <- function(model, train, test) {
  d <- fill_missing(train, test)
  predict_model(fit_model(model, d$train), d$test)
}
```

### 8-2. Fit all the models on all of `raw` and look at them

```{r fit-all}
fits <- lapply(MODELS, function(m) fit_model(m, dat))
names(fits) <- MODELS

fitted_long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(MODELS, function(m)
  data.frame(model = m, actual = dat[[TARGET]], fitted = predict_model(fits[[m]], dat))))
fitted_long$model <- factor(fitted_long$model, levels = MODELS)

# Actual vs fitted: the points should lie on the red line
ggplot(fitted_long, aes(x = fitted, y = actual)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5) + geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ model) + labs(x = "fitted", y = "actual", title = "Actual vs fitted (all of raw)")

# Residuals vs fitted: the points should scatter evenly around 0
ggplot(fitted_long, aes(x = fitted, y = actual - fitted)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ model) + labs(x = "fitted", y = "residual (actual - fitted)", title = "Residuals vs fitted (all of raw)")
```

```{r coef-plots}
# lasso and ridge: the coefficients (on the scale of the transformed y). A lasso coefficient of exactly 0 = the variable is dropped.
coefs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("lasso", "ridge"), function(m) {
  cf <- as.matrix(coef(fits[[m]]$fit, s = "lambda.min"))
  data.frame(model = m, term = rownames(cf), coef = cf[, 1])
}))
coefs <- coefs[coefs$term != "(Intercept)", ]
ggplot(coefs, aes(x = term, y = coef)) +
  geom_col() + coord_flip() + facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(x = "term", y = "coefficient", title = "lasso and ridge coefficients")

# mixed model: the random intercept of every group (how much higher / lower the group is than the average)
if (!is.null(GROUP)) {
  re_df <- data.frame(group = rownames(lme4::ranef(fits$mixed$fit)[[GROUP]]), effect = lme4::ranef(fits$mixed$fit)[[GROUP]][, 1])
  ggplot(re_df, aes(x = reorder(group, effect), y = effect)) +
    geom_point() + coord_flip() +
    labs(x = GROUP, y = "random intercept", title = "mixed model: the effect of every group")
}
```

## 9. Model comparison: the moving window

The models are compared on rows they **did not see**. With a time column: the model is trained on the last `WINDOW` days, predicts the next `TEST_DAYS` days, and the window moves forward; all the predictions are collected and then scored. Without a time column: K-fold.

The 5 scores (computed on **y in its own units**, after the transformation is turned back):

| score | meaning |
|---|---|
| `RMSE` | the typical error; big errors count more. Smaller is better |
| `MAE` | the average of the absolute errors. Smaller is better |
| `MAPE` | the average error in % of y (rows with y = 0 are left out). Smaller is better |
| `R2` | 1 = perfect, 0 = as good as the mean of y, negative = worse than the mean. Larger is better |
| `Bias` | the average of (prediction - actual): positive = the model predicts too high. Close to 0 is good |

```{r cv-tools}
metrics <- function(y, p) {
  e <- p - y
  c(RMSE = sqrt(mean(e^2)),
    MAE  = mean(abs(e)),
    MAPE = 100 * mean(abs(e[y != 0]) / abs(y[y != 0])),
    R2   = 1 - sum(e^2) / sum((y - mean(y))^2),
    Bias = mean(e))
}

# The moving window: for every block of TEST_DAYS days from `from` to `to`, train on the WINDOW days before the block and predict the block
run_sliding <- function(model, data, from, to) {
  out   <- NULL
  start <- from
  while (start <= to) {
    end   <- min(start + TEST_DAYS - 1, to)
    train <- data[data$.day >= start - WINDOW & data$.day < start, ]
    test  <- data[data$.day >= start & data$.day <= end, ]
    train <- train[!is.na(train[[TARGET]]), ]
    test  <- test[!is.na(test[[TARGET]]), ]
    if (nrow(train) > 0 && nrow(test) > 0) {
      out <- rbind(out, data.frame(day = test$.day, y = test[[TARGET]], pred = fit_predict(model, train, test)))
    }
    start <- end + 1
  }
  out
}

# Without a time column: K-fold on raw
run_kfold <- function(model) {
  set.seed(SEED)
  fold <- sample(rep(1:FOLDS, length.out = nrow(raw)))
  out  <- NULL
  for (k in 1:FOLDS) {
    test <- raw[fold == k, ]
    out  <- rbind(out, data.frame(y = test[[TARGET]], pred = fit_predict(model, raw[fold != k, ], test)))
  }
  out
}

run_cv <- function(model) {
  if (HAS_TIME) run_sliding(model, raw, from = min(raw$.day) + WINDOW, to = max(raw$.day)) else run_kfold(model)
}
```

```{r cv-run}
if (HAS_TIME) stopifnot("raw has fewer days than WINDOW: lower WINDOW in the settings" = as.numeric(max(raw$.day) - min(raw$.day)) > WINDOW)
cv_pred <- list()
for (m in MODELS) { cv_pred[[m]] <- run_cv(m); cat(m, "") }       # (this takes a while: one fit for every model and every block)
cat("\n")

cv_table <- t(sapply(cv_pred, function(p) metrics(p$y, p$pred)))
cv_table <- cv_table[order(cv_table[, "RMSE"]), ]
round(cv_table, 3)
```

```{r cv-plot}
# the RMSE of every model (smaller is better)
cv_df <- data.frame(model = rownames(cv_table), RMSE = cv_table[, "RMSE"])
ggplot(cv_df, aes(x = reorder(model, RMSE), y = RMSE)) +
  geom_col() + labs(x = "model", y = "RMSE", title = "Moving window: RMSE of every model")

m = "glm"
# actual vs predicted of every model (the predictions the models made for rows they did not see)
cv_long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(cv_pred), function(m) data.frame(model = m, y = cv_pred[[m]]$y, pred = cv_pred[[m]]$pred)))
ggplot(cv_long, aes(x = pred, y = y)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.4) + geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ model) + labs(x = "predicted", y = "actual", title = "Moving window: actual vs predicted")
```

## 10. The holdout (once)

**Open the holdout only when the analysis above is finished.** Same rule as in section 9: the models are trained on the last `WINDOW` days before every block of `TEST_DAYS` days of the holdout (the days of the holdout that are already past are used as training days, as in real life). Nothing is chosen with these numbers: they only tell how good the final model really is.

```{r holdout}
holdout <- readRDS("holdout.rds")

if (HAS_TIME) {
  holdout$.day <- as.Date(holdout[[TIME]])
  full <- rbind(raw, holdout)                                                   # raw followed by holdout
  hold_pred <- lapply(MODELS, function(m) run_sliding(m, full, from = min(holdout$.day), to = max(holdout$.day)))
} else {
  hold_pred <- lapply(MODELS, function(m) data.frame(y = holdout[[TARGET]], pred = fit_predict(m, raw, holdout)))   # trained on all of raw
}
names(hold_pred) <- MODELS

hold_table <- t(sapply(hold_pred, function(p) metrics(p$y, p$pred)))
hold_table <- hold_table[order(hold_table[, "RMSE"]), ]
round(hold_table, 3)
```

```{r holdout-plot}
# actual vs predicted of every model
best = "glm"
hold_long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(hold_pred), function(m) data.frame(model = m, y = hold_pred[[m]]$y, pred = hold_pred[[m]]$pred)))
ggplot(hold_long, aes(x = pred, y = y)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.4) + geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ model) + labs(x = "predicted", y = "actual", title = "Holdout: actual vs predicted")

# over time: the daily mean of the actual y and of the prediction of the best model
if (HAS_TIME) {
  best <- rownames(hold_table)[1]
  p    <- hold_pred[[best]]
  actual <- stats::aggregate(y ~ day, data = p, FUN = base::mean)
  predicted <- stats::aggregate(pred ~ day, data = p, FUN = base::mean)

daily <- rbind(
  data.frame(day = actual$day, value = actual$y, what = "actual"),
  data.frame(day = predicted$day, value = predicted$pred, what = "predicted")
)
  ggplot(daily, aes(x = day, y = value, color = what)) +
    geom_line() + labs(x = "day", y = paste("daily mean of", TARGET), title = paste("Holdout over time:", best))
}

newp <- p |> group_by(day) |> summarise(mean_y = mean(y), mean_yhat = mean(pred))

newp |> ggplot(aes(x = day))+
  geom_line(aes(y = mean_y), color = "red") +
  geom_line(aes(y = mean_yhat), color = "blue")

newp |> ggplot(aes(x = day, y = mean_yhat - mean_y)) + geom_line()
```

# Part B. Classification (the TARGET is a category)

Use Part B when the outcome is a **category**: 0 / 1 (two classes), 1, 2, ..., K (several classes) or text. **Run Part B instead of Part A** (not after it): it has its own settings, and it starts from the same files of the EDA template (`raw.rds`, `roles.rds` and, at the very end, `holdout.rds`). The same code handles two classes and several classes (`BINARY` is `TRUE` for two classes).

**Contents of Part B**

- B-0. Packages and settings
- B-1. Load `raw` (and an example: a category made from a number)
- B-2. Missing values
- B-3. Variable selection (forward / backward, AIC / BIC)
- B-4. Check the assumptions
- B-5. A light try: transform the numeric x
- B-6. Outliers (and how they differ from the normal rows)
- B-7. Interactions
- B-8. The models, fitted on all of `raw`, and their plots
- B-9. Model comparison: moving window (train = the last 60 days)
- B-10. The holdout (once)

- Same steps as Part A, with a logistic regression instead of an lm. **There is no Box-Cox:** the target is not a number.
- **You decide the analysis.** The places where you decide are marked `# <-- YOUR DECISION`: `SELECTED` (B-3), `X_TRANS` (B-5), `OUTLIER_COL` (B-6), `COLUMN1` / `COLUMN2` / `INTER_ADD` (B-7).
- **Time series is the default** (same as Part A): the models are trained on the last `WINDOW` days before the days they predict. Without a time column K-fold is used.
- The EDA template does not know that the TARGET is a category: ignore what does not fit (for example the numeric statistics of the target). It only has to write `raw.rds`, `holdout.rds` and `roles.rds`.

**What to change for a new data set (and where it is)**

| what | where |
|---|---|
| `TARGET` (a category), `TIME` (`NULL` = no time column), `GROUP` (`NULL` = none) | chunk `b-settings` (B-0): the three required settings |
| the class that counts as "positive" (two classes), the cut-off of the probability | `b-settings`: `POSITIVE`, `THRESHOLD` |
| the length of the moving window, the number of days predicted at once | `b-settings`: `WINDOW`, `TEST_DAYS` |
| a category made from a number (example only) | B-1, chunk `b-demo-target`: **delete it** if your TARGET is already a category |
| the numeric / categorical predictors | the EDA template wrote them to `roles.rds`. To use your own lists, write `NUM <- c(...)` and `CAT <- c(...)` in chunk `b-load-raw` |
| which variable-selection result | B-3, chunk `b-select-final`: `SELECTED` |
| which transformations of the x | B-5, chunk `b-x-trans`: `X_TRANS` |
| which column is checked for outliers, and the rule | B-6, chunk `b-outlier-check`: `OUTLIER_COL`, `K_IQR`, `OUTLIER_BY` |
| which interactions | B-7: option 1 = chunk `b-inter-test` (`COLUMN1`, `COLUMN2`, then `b-inter-add`), option 2 = chunks `b-inter-scan` and `b-inter-scan-add` (`INTER_ADD`). Both fill `INTER_SEL` |

| name | meaning |
|---|---|
| `CLASSES` | the classes of the target, for example `"1" "2" "3"` |
| `BINARY` | `TRUE` if there are two classes |
| the others | the same as in Part A: `raw`, `holdout`, `dat` (raw with the missing values filled), `full` (raw followed by holdout), `NUM`, `CAT` |

## B-0. Packages and settings

```{r b-settings}
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "glmnet", "lme4", "nnet", "rpart", "MASS", "car", "pROC"))     # run once if a package is missing
library(tidyverse)
options(width = 150)

# ===== Settings =====
SEED       <- 0
TARGET     <- "demand_class"       # the outcome (y): a category. 0 / 1, 1..K or text. (The example below makes it from rentals)
TIME       <- "date"               # the time column. NULL if the data has no time column
GROUP      <- "station_id"         # a column whose values repeat (the same station / customer ...). NULL if none

POSITIVE   <- NULL                 # two classes: the class that counts as "positive" (NULL = the last class, for 0 / 1 it is 1)
THRESHOLD  <- 0.5                  # two classes: a row is predicted "positive" if its probability is larger than this. A smaller number finds more positives

WINDOW     <- 60                   # moving window: the models are trained on the last 60 days before the days they predict
TEST_DAYS  <- 7                    # ... and predict the next 7 days, then the window moves forward by 7 days
FOLDS      <- 5                    # K-fold (only used when there is no time column)
# ====================

HAS_TIME <- !is.null(TIME)
set.seed(SEED)
```

## B-1. Load `raw`

```{r b-load-raw}
raw   <- readRDS("raw.rds")         # written by the EDA template (section 11-4)
roles <- readRDS("roles.rds")
NUM   <- roles$NUM                  # numeric predictors   (your own list: NUM <- c("temp_c", "rain_mm"))
CAT   <- roles$CAT                  # categorical predictors (your own list: CAT <- c("station_type"))

if (HAS_TIME) {
  raw <- raw[order(raw[[TIME]]), ]
  raw$.day <- as.Date(raw[[TIME]])  # the day of every row (the moving window works with days)
}
```

**Example only: a category target made from a number.** The bike data has a numeric outcome (`rentals`). To have something to classify, the chunk below cuts it into classes `1, 2, ..., N_DEMO` (low ... high) at quantiles **of `raw`**; the holdout gets the same cut-offs (section B-10). **If your own TARGET is already a category (0 / 1, 1..K or text), delete this chunk** and write its name in `TARGET` in the settings.

```{r b-demo-target}
NUMERIC_Y  <- "rentals"                                   # the numeric column the category is made from
N_DEMO     <- 3                                           # the number of classes (2 = low / high, 3 = low / mid / high ...)
CUTS       <- quantile(raw[[NUMERIC_Y]], (1:(N_DEMO - 1)) / N_DEMO, na.rm = TRUE)     # the cut-offs: learned on raw only
make_class <- function(d) as.integer(cut(d[[NUMERIC_Y]], c(-Inf, CUTS, Inf)))        # 1, 2, ..., N_DEMO
raw[[TARGET]] <- make_class(raw)
NUM <- setdiff(NUM, NUMERIC_Y)                            # the number the category was made from must not be a predictor
CAT <- setdiff(CAT, NUMERIC_Y)
```

```{r b-classes}
NUM <- setdiff(NUM, TARGET)                               # the target is not a predictor
CAT <- setdiff(CAT, TARGET)
stopifnot(all(c(TARGET, NUM, CAT, GROUP) %in% names(raw)))

# The classes of the target. The same order is used everywhere (also for the holdout).
raw <- raw[!is.na(raw[[TARGET]]), ]
CLASSES <- levels(factor(raw[[TARGET]]))
BINARY  <- length(CLASSES) == 2
if (BINARY && is.null(POSITIVE)) POSITIVE <- CLASSES[2]
raw[[TARGET]] <- factor(raw[[TARGET]], levels = CLASSES)

cat("raw:", nrow(raw), "rows | numeric predictors:", length(NUM), "| categorical predictors:", length(CAT), "\n")
cat("classes:", CLASSES, if (BINARY) paste("| positive class:", POSITIVE) else "(several classes)", "\n")
round(table(raw[[TARGET]]) / nrow(raw), 3)            # the share of every class: a very small class is hard to predict
```

## B-2. Missing values

A model cannot use a row that has a missing value. **The EDA template filled the missing values of the predictors once, for `raw` and `holdout` together** (its section 11, the last one: it fills the missing values on all the rows, makes the new columns, and writes the files `raw.rds` and `holdout.rds`). The method was chosen there (`METHOD`: `"time_window"` = the median of the last `WINDOW_DAYS` days before the row, `"all"` = the median of the raw rows, and others). So here there is usually **nothing left to fill**: the chunk below checks it.

The function `fill_missing()` stays as a **safety net**, and it is used again inside every model of sections B-8 to B-10:

1. a value that is still missing (for example if section 11 of the EDA template was not run) is filled with the **median of the training rows** (a categorical column: the new category `"Missing"`, or the most frequent category if there was no missing value in the training rows);
2. the categories are made the same in train and test (a category that is not in train becomes the filler).

The outcome (`TARGET`) is never filled.

```{r b-fill-missing}
most_common <- function(x) names(sort(table(x), decreasing = TRUE))[1]

fill_missing <- function(train, test) {
  for (col in NUM) {
    m <- median(train[[col]], na.rm = TRUE)               # the median of the TRAIN rows
    train[[col]][is.na(train[[col]])] <- m
    test[[col]][is.na(test[[col]])]   <- m
  }
  for (col in CAT) {
    train[[col]] <- as.character(train[[col]])
    test[[col]]  <- as.character(test[[col]])
    fill <- if (any(is.na(train[[col]]))) "Missing" else most_common(train[[col]])
    train[[col]][is.na(train[[col]])] <- fill
    test[[col]][is.na(test[[col]]) | !(test[[col]] %in% train[[col]])] <- fill    # NA, or a category that is not in train
    train[[col]] <- factor(train[[col]])
    test[[col]]  <- factor(test[[col]], levels = levels(train[[col]]))             # the same levels in train and test
  }
  list(train = train, test = test)
}

# For the sections before the models: a copy of raw, with anything that is still missing filled
dat <- fill_missing(raw, raw)$train

colSums(is.na(raw[c(NUM, CAT)]))                          # missing values in the predictors of raw (all 0 after section 11 of the EDA template)
sum(is.na(dat[c(NUM, CAT)]))                              # ... and in dat
if (any(is.na(raw[c(NUM, CAT)]))) cat("There are still missing values: run section 11 of the EDA template (or leave them: fill_missing() fills them with the median of the training rows)\n")
```

## B-3. Variable selection (forward / backward, AIC / BIC)

Four ways to select the variables of a **logistic regression** (two classes: `glm`; several classes: `nnet::multinom`):

- **forward**: start from no variable and add the variable that helps most, until nothing helps;
- **backward**: start from all variables and remove the one that hurts least, until every one is needed;
- **AIC** keeps more variables, **BIC** keeps fewer (a bigger penalty for every variable).

```{r b-select-four}
if (BINARY) {
  m_null <- glm(reformulate("1", TARGET),            family = binomial, data = dat)
  m_full <- glm(reformulate(c(NUM, CAT), TARGET),    family = binomial, data = dat)
} else {
  m_null <- nnet::multinom(reformulate("1", TARGET),         data = dat, trace = FALSE)
  m_full <- nnet::multinom(reformulate(c(NUM, CAT), TARGET), data = dat, trace = FALSE)
}
n <- nrow(dat)

up  <- list(lower = ~ 1, upper = formula(m_full))
sel <- list(
  forward_AIC  = MASS::stepAIC(m_null, scope = up, direction = "forward",  trace = FALSE),
  forward_BIC  = MASS::stepAIC(m_null, scope = up, direction = "forward",  trace = FALSE, k = log(n)),
  backward_AIC = MASS::stepAIC(m_full, direction = "backward", trace = FALSE),
  backward_BIC = MASS::stepAIC(m_full, direction = "backward", trace = FALSE, k = log(n)))
sel$full <- m_full

# the four results and the full model side by side
data.frame(n_terms = sapply(sel, function(m) length(attr(terms(m), "term.labels"))),
           AIC     = round(sapply(sel, AIC), 1),
           BIC     = round(sapply(sel, BIC), 1))

for (nm in names(sel)) cat(nm, ":", attr(terms(sel[[nm]]), "term.labels"), "\n\n")
```

```{r b-select-final}
SELECTED <- "forward_AIC"      # <-- YOUR DECISION: "forward_AIC" | "forward_BIC" | "backward_AIC" | "backward_BIC" | "full"

formula_sel <- formula(sel[[SELECTED]])                  # the selected formula: everything below is built on it
sel_terms   <- attr(terms(formula_sel), "term.labels")   # its terms
formula_sel
```

## B-4. Check the assumptions

A logistic regression does not need normal residuals. What matters: enough rows in every class, predictors that are not copies of each other, a straight-line relation between a numeric x and the **log-odds**, and no single row that pulls the fit.

```{r b-assumptions}
# 1 The classes: a class with very few rows is hard to learn
barplot(table(dat[[TARGET]]), main = paste("Rows in every class of", TARGET), xlab = TARGET, ylab = "count")

# 2 Variance inflation factor: larger than 5-10 = the variable is explained by the other variables (it does not depend on the target)
vif_fit <- lm(reformulate(sel_terms, ".code"), data = transform(dat, .code = as.integer(dat[[TARGET]])))
tryCatch(car::vif(vif_fit), error = function(e) "VIF cannot be computed: some columns are explained by the others (aliased). Look for two variables with the same information.")

num_in <- intersect(NUM, all.vars(formula_sel))                      # the numeric variables of the selected formula

if (BINARY) {
  # 3 Is the log-odds a straight line in x? The rows are cut in 10 groups of x; the points should lie roughly on a straight line
  y01 <- as.integer(dat[[TARGET]] == POSITIVE)
  par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
  for (x in head(num_in[sapply(dat[num_in], n_distinct) > 2], 4)) {
    cuts <- unique(quantile(dat[[x]], seq(0, 1, 0.1)))
    if (length(cuts) < 3) next
    grp  <- cut(dat[[x]], cuts, include.lowest = TRUE)
    p    <- tapply(y01, grp, mean)
    plot(tapply(dat[[x]], grp, mean), log((p + 0.01) / (1 - p + 0.01)), xlab = x, ylab = "log-odds of the positive class", main = x)
  }
  par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

  # 4 Cook's distance: a few very tall bars are rows that pull the fit
  plot(glm(formula_sel, family = binomial, data = dat), which = 4)
}
```

## B-5. A light try: transform the numeric x

For every numeric variable of the selected formula: does adding `x^2`, `log(x)`, `sqrt(x)` or `exp(x)` help? A negative `AIC_change` = better. A small `p_value` = the new term is useful.

```{r b-x-trans}
fit_terms <- function(terms) {                              # a logistic regression with these terms
  f <- reformulate(terms, TARGET)
  if (BINARY) glm(f, family = binomial, data = dat) else nnet::multinom(f, data = dat, trace = FALSE)
}
m_sel <- fit_terms(sel_terms)

tried <- NULL
for (x in num_in) {
  v <- dat[[x]]
  if (n_distinct(v) <= 2) next                              # a 0/1 variable: nothing to transform
  terms_try <- paste0("I(", x, "^2)")                       # x squared
  if (min(v) > 0)  terms_try <- c(terms_try, paste0("log(", x, ")"))     # only possible for positive x
  if (min(v) >= 0) terms_try <- c(terms_try, paste0("sqrt(", x, ")"))    # only possible for x >= 0
  if (max(v) < 20) terms_try <- c(terms_try, paste0("exp(", x, ")"))     # (a big x makes exp(x) explode)
  for (tt in terms_try) {
    m2    <- fit_terms(c(sel_terms, tt))
    lr    <- 2 * (as.numeric(logLik(m2)) - as.numeric(logLik(m_sel)))                 # likelihood-ratio test of the new term
    df_lr <- attr(logLik(m2), "df") - attr(logLik(m_sel), "df")
    tried <- rbind(tried, data.frame(term = tt, AIC_change = round(AIC(m2) - AIC(m_sel), 1), p_value = round(pchisq(lr, df_lr, lower.tail = FALSE), 4)))
  }
}
if (!is.null(tried)) tried[order(tried$AIC_change), ]

X_TRANS <- character(0)      # <-- YOUR DECISION: the terms you want to add, for example c("I(temp_c^2)", "log(rain_mm + 1)"). character(0) = none
```

## B-6. Outliers

An outlier is a row whose value is very far from the others. Before the interactions we look at two things: (1) which rows are the outliers of a numeric column, (2) **how they differ from the normal rows**: the other numeric columns, the categories, and **the class of the TARGET** (are the outliers mostly in one class?). This is the same idea as "what does the missingness mean?" in the EDA template (its section 9).

The rule (Tukey, the whiskers of a boxplot): a value is an outlier if it is below `Q1 - K_IQR * IQR` or above `Q3 + K_IQR * IQR`. The checked column `OUTLIER_COL` is a numeric predictor (the TARGET is a category: it has no outliers).

Nothing is removed from `dat`: this section only looks. Run the chunk again with another `OUTLIER_COL` to check another column.

```{r b-outlier-check}
# ===== What to check: CHANGE HERE, then run this chunk (run it again for another column) =====
OUTLIER_COL <- NUM[1]      # <-- CHANGE HERE: a numeric column, for example "temp_c"
K_IQR       <- 1.5         # <-- CHANGE HERE (optional): 1.5 = the usual outliers, 3 = only the extreme ones
OUTLIER_BY  <- NULL        # <-- CHANGE HERE (optional): NULL = all the rows together. A column (for example GROUP) = the rule is applied inside every value of that column
# ==========================================================================================

stopifnot("OUTLIER_COL must be a numeric column of dat" = OUTLIER_COL %in% names(dat) && is.numeric(dat[[OUTLIER_COL]]))

x   <- dat[[OUTLIER_COL]]
grp <- if (is.null(OUTLIER_BY)) rep(1, nrow(dat)) else dat[[OUTLIER_BY]]
q1  <- ave(x, grp, FUN = function(v) quantile(v, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE))      # the quartiles (of every group if OUTLIER_BY is used)
q3  <- ave(x, grp, FUN = function(v) quantile(v, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE))
lo  <- q1 - K_IQR * (q3 - q1)                                              # below this = a low outlier
hi  <- q3 + K_IQR * (q3 - q1)                                              # above this = a high outlier
is_out <- (x < lo | x > hi) %in% TRUE                                      # TRUE = outlier (a missing value is not an outlier)

cat(OUTLIER_COL, ": ", sum(is_out), " outliers in ", length(x), " rows (", round(100 * mean(is_out), 1), "%) | low: ", sum(x < lo, na.rm = TRUE), " | high: ", sum(x > hi, na.rm = TRUE), "\n", sep = "")

# ----- the pictures -----
boxplot(x, main = paste("Boxplot of", OUTLIER_COL), ylab = OUTLIER_COL)    # the dots are the outliers (same rule when OUTLIER_BY = NULL and K_IQR = 1.5)
if (HAS_TIME) {                                                            # when are they? (red = outlier)
  plot(dat$.day, x, pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = ifelse(is_out, "red", "grey40"),
       main = paste(OUTLIER_COL, "over time (red = outlier)"), xlab = "day", ylab = OUTLIER_COL)
}

# ----- how are the outliers different from the normal rows? -----
if (sum(is_out) > 0 && sum(!is_out) > 0) {
  # 1. numeric columns: the mean in the outlier group and in the normal group
  comp_num  <- setdiff(NUM, OUTLIER_COL)                                             # the other numeric columns
  mean_out  <- sapply(dat[is_out,  comp_num, drop = FALSE], mean, na.rm = TRUE)
  mean_norm <- sapply(dat[!is_out, comp_num, drop = FALSE], mean, na.rm = TRUE)
  std_diff  <- (mean_out - mean_norm) / sapply(dat[comp_num], sd, na.rm = TRUE)      # (mean of the outliers - mean of the normal rows) / overall sd: below 0.2 tiny, above 0.8 large
  num_tab   <- data.frame(mean_outlier = mean_out, mean_normal = mean_norm, std_diff = round(std_diff, 3))
  print(round(num_tab[order(-abs(num_tab$std_diff)), ], 3))                          # the biggest differences first

  # 2. categories (the classes of the TARGET too): the share of outliers in every category (compare it with the overall share)
  cat("\nthe overall share of outliers:", round(100 * mean(is_out), 1), "%\n")
  cat_cols  <- unique(c(CAT, GROUP, TARGET))
  share_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(cat_cols, function(v) {
    g     <- as.character(dat[[v]]);  g[is.na(g)] <- "NA"
    n_all <- tapply(is_out, g, length)
    n_out <- tapply(is_out, g, sum)
    data.frame(variable = v, level = names(n_all), n = as.vector(n_all), n_outlier = as.vector(n_out),
               pct_outlier = round(100 * as.vector(n_out) / as.vector(n_all), 1))
  }))
  share_tab <- share_tab[share_tab$n >= 5, ]                                         # tiny categories are left out
  share_tab <- share_tab[order(-share_tab$pct_outlier), ]
  rownames(share_tab) <- NULL
  print(head(share_tab, 15))                                                         # the 15 categories with the highest share of outliers

  # 3. over time: the share of outliers in every month
  if (HAS_TIME) print(round(100 * tapply(is_out, format(dat$.day, "%Y-%m"), mean), 1))
} else cat("\nthere are no outliers (or no normal rows): nothing to compare\n")
```

**How to read the result**

- `std_diff` (numeric columns): the difference of the two means in units of the overall standard deviation (below 0.2: tiny, above 0.8: large). `pct_outlier` (categories): the share of outliers inside the category: compare it with the overall share printed above the table. The rows with `variable` = the TARGET tell whether the outliers are mostly in one class.
- **A clear pattern** (a large `std_diff`, or a category or a class with a much higher share) = the outliers are **explained by a variable**. Keep the rows and give the model what it misses: that variable (B-3), a transformation (B-5) or an **interaction** (the next section).
- **No pattern**: the outliers look random (a data error? a one-off event?). Look at the rows (`dat[is_out, ]`) before you decide to leave them.

## B-7. Interactions

An interaction `a:b` means: the effect of `a` is different for different values of `b`. There are **two options**, and both fill the same list `INTER_SEL` (the interactions you keep). Use one of them, or both, as many times as you like. (Outliers that are explained by two variables together, section B-6, are a good reason to test that pair.)

- **OPTION 1: you choose the pair.** Write `COLUMN1` and `COLUMN2` (any two columns of `dat`, numeric or categorical), run the test, **look at the result, and decide**: run the chunk `b-inter-add` to add the pair, or skip it. Then go back to `COLUMN1` / `COLUMN2` and test the next pair.
- **OPTION 2: scan.** The variables of the selected formula are tried in pairs, **one interaction at a time**, and the table shows the pairs with the smallest p-value. You write the ones you want in `INTER_ADD`.

With many pairs (option 2) a few small p-values come by chance: prefer the very small ones that also make sense. The test is the likelihood-ratio test of the logistic regression (`glm`; several classes: `nnet::multinom`, which can take a while).

```{r b-inter-start}
# Run this chunk ONCE (it empties INTER_SEL): do NOT run it again after you have added interactions.
RHS       <- c(sel_terms, X_TRANS)                                          # the terms until now
INTER_SEL <- character(0)                                                   # the interactions kept (OPTION 1 and OPTION 2 add to it)
RHS_FINAL <- unique(c(RHS, unlist(strsplit(INTER_SEL, ":")), INTER_SEL))    # THE FORMULA FROM NOW ON (an interaction brings the main effects of its two columns)
```

### OPTION 1: test the pair you choose

The chunks of option 1 name specific columns (`temp_c`, `station_type` ...), so they are `eval = FALSE`: **they are not run when you knit**. Write your own columns and run them by hand. (They use `fit_terms()` of the chunk `b-x-trans`: run that chunk first.)

```{r b-inter-test, eval=FALSE}
# ===== The pair to test: CHANGE HERE, then run this chunk =====
COLUMN1 <- "temp_c"            # <-- CHANGE HERE: any column (numeric or categorical)
COLUMN2 <- "station_type"      # <-- CHANGE HERE: another column (numeric or categorical)
# ==============================================================

stopifnot("COLUMN1 and COLUMN2 must be two different columns" = COLUMN1 != COLUMN2,
          "COLUMN1 and COLUMN2 must be columns of dat"        = all(c(COLUMN1, COLUMN2) %in% names(dat)))
INTER_TEST <- paste(COLUMN1, COLUMN2, sep = ":")                            # "a:b"
same_inter <- c(INTER_TEST, paste(COLUMN2, COLUMN1, sep = ":"))             # "a:b" and "b:a" are the same interaction
inter_keep <- setdiff(INTER_SEL, same_inter)                                # the interactions kept before (without this one: it is the one tested)
base_terms <- unique(c(RHS, COLUMN1, COLUMN2, unlist(strsplit(inter_keep, ":")), inter_keep))   # the model WITHOUT this interaction (the main effects of both columns are in)

# A column that never changes inside a group (a station's capacity ...): the interaction of TWO such columns only builds the group ID again
if (!is.null(GROUP) && all(sapply(c(COLUMN1, COLUMN2), function(v) all(tapply(dat[[v]], dat[[GROUP]], n_distinct) == 1)))) {
  cat("WARNING: both columns never change inside a", GROUP, ": the p-value is meaningless\n")
}

# Likelihood-ratio test in the logistic regression: a small p-value = the interaction helps
fit0  <- fit_terms(base_terms)
fit1  <- fit_terms(c(base_terms, INTER_TEST))
lr    <- 2 * (as.numeric(logLik(fit1)) - as.numeric(logLik(fit0)))          # how much better the fit gets
df_lr <- attr(logLik(fit1), "df") - attr(logLik(fit0), "df")                # how many parameters were added
p_lr  <- pchisq(lr, df_lr, lower.tail = FALSE)
print(data.frame(Df = df_lr, AIC_change = round(AIC(fit1) - AIC(fit0), 1), LR = round(lr, 2), p_value = signif(p_lr, 3)), row.names = FALSE)
cat("\n", INTER_TEST, ": p-value =", signif(p_lr, 3), "  -> add it? run the chunk b-inter-add (or skip it)\n")
```

#### (optional) The same pair in a mixed model (two classes)

The **same** pair (`COLUMN1`, `COLUMN2`) in a mixed model (a random intercept per group), to help you decide. It only shows the numbers.

```{r b-inter-other, eval=FALSE}
if (BINARY && !is.null(GROUP)) {
  re <- paste0("(1 | ", GROUP, ")")                         # a random intercept per group
  m0 <- lme4::glmer(reformulate(c(base_terms, re), TARGET),               family = binomial, data = dat)
  m1 <- lme4::glmer(reformulate(c(base_terms, INTER_TEST, re), TARGET),   family = binomial, data = dat)
  anova(m0, m1)                                             # a small p-value = the interaction helps
}
```

#### Add the pair (only if you want it)

```{r b-inter-add, eval=FALSE}
# Run this chunk ONLY if you want the pair of the LAST run of b-inter-test (INTER_TEST). To leave the pair out: do not run it.
INTER_SEL <- unique(c(setdiff(INTER_SEL, same_inter), INTER_TEST))              # (the same pair in the other order is replaced, not repeated)
RHS_FINAL <- unique(c(RHS, unlist(strsplit(INTER_SEL, ":")), INTER_SEL))        # THE FORMULA FROM NOW ON
# To take one out later:  INTER_SEL <- setdiff(INTER_SEL, "a:b")   and run the RHS_FINAL line again

INTER_SEL          # the interactions kept so far
RHS_FINAL          # the formula from now on
```

### OPTION 2: scan the pairs of the selected variables

```{r b-inter-scan}
# Which variables are tried in pairs?  FALSE: the variables of the selected formula.  TRUE: ALL the variables of NUM and CAT.
# (A variable can matter only through an interaction: its own effect cancels out, so section B-3 may have dropped it. TRUE finds such a variable.)
SCAN_ALL <- FALSE
vars <- if (SCAN_ALL) c(NUM, CAT) else all.vars(formula_sel)[-1]
terms_base <- unique(c(RHS, vars))                          # the main effects of all these variables
m_ref <- fit_terms(terms_base)                              # the model without any interaction

# A variable that never changes inside a group (a station's capacity ...) can only separate the groups. The interaction of TWO such variables
# only builds the group ID again (the group effect of section B-8 does that already, and the p-value is meaningless): leave those pairs out.
group_level <- setNames(rep(FALSE, length(vars)), vars)
if (!is.null(GROUP)) group_level <- sapply(vars, function(v) all(tapply(dat[[v]], dat[[GROUP]], n_distinct) == 1))

pair_terms <- NULL
if (length(vars) >= 2) {
  all_pairs  <- combn(vars, 2, simplify = FALSE)                          # all pairs of variables
  ok_pairs   <- Filter(function(p) !all(group_level[p]), all_pairs)       # without the pairs of two group-level variables
  pair_terms <- sapply(ok_pairs, paste, collapse = ":")                   # "a:b"
}

# Every pair is added to the model, one at a time, and tested with the likelihood-ratio test.
# (With several classes every pair is a new fit of a bigger model: this can take a minute or two.)
inter_tab <- NULL
for (pt in pair_terms) {
  m2 <- tryCatch(fit_terms(c(terms_base, pt)), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(m2)) next
  lr    <- 2 * (as.numeric(logLik(m2)) - as.numeric(logLik(m_ref)))                  # how much better the fit gets
  df_lr <- attr(logLik(m2), "df") - attr(logLik(m_ref), "df")                         # how many parameters were added
  inter_tab <- rbind(inter_tab, data.frame(pair = pt, Df = df_lr, AIC = round(AIC(m2), 1), p_value = pchisq(lr, df_lr, lower.tail = FALSE)))
}
if (!is.null(inter_tab)) {
  rownames(inter_tab) <- inter_tab$pair
  inter_tab <- inter_tab[order(inter_tab$p_value), c("Df", "AIC", "p_value")]         # a small p-value = the interaction helps
  round(head(inter_tab, 15), 4)                                                       # the 15 pairs with the smallest p-value
}
```

```{r b-inter-scan-add}
INTER_ADD <- character(0)    # <-- YOUR DECISION: the interactions of the table above to add, for example c("day_off:station_type"). character(0) = none
INTER_SEL <- c(INTER_SEL, INTER_ADD)
pair_key  <- vapply(strsplit(INTER_SEL, ":"), function(p) paste(sort(p), collapse = ":"), character(1))   # "a:b" and "b:a" are the same interaction
INTER_SEL <- INTER_SEL[!duplicated(pair_key)]                                                            # keep it only once
RHS_FINAL <- unique(c(RHS, unlist(strsplit(INTER_SEL, ":")), INTER_SEL))    # THE FORMULA FROM NOW ON (an interaction brings the main effects of its two variables)

INTER_SEL
RHS_FINAL
```

## B-8. The models

### B-8-1. The tools (you do not need to change them)

Every model is built from **the same terms** (`RHS_FINAL`). Two functions do everything:

- `fit_model(model, train)` fits a model on the training rows;
- `predict_model(obj, test)` gives, for every test row, the **probability of every class** (a table with one column per class).

| model | what it is |
|---|---|
| `baseline` | the share of every class in the training rows: the number to beat |
| `logit` | logistic regression (`glm`; several classes: `multinom`) |
| `lasso` | logistic regression that shrinks the coefficients; some become exactly 0 |
| `ridge` | logistic regression that shrinks the coefficients; none becomes 0 |
| `tree` | a decision tree (`rpart`): easy to read |
| `glmm` | logistic regression + a random intercept per `GROUP` (**two classes only**) |

A group (station) that is not in the training rows gets the average effect. If a model cannot be fitted (for example a class with 1 row in the window) the baseline is used and counted in `n_fallback`.

```{r b-tools}
MODELS <- c("baseline", "logit", "lasso", "ridge", "tree", if (BINARY && !is.null(GROUP)) "glmm")
n_fallback <- 0

# keep only the terms whose variables have at least 2 different values in the training rows
keep_terms <- function(terms, tr) {
  ok <- sapply(terms, function(t) all(sapply(all.vars(parse(text = t)[[1]]), function(v) n_distinct(tr[[v]]) > 1)))
  if (any(ok)) terms[ok] else "1"
}

fit_model <- function(model, tr) {
  tr[[TARGET]] <- droplevels(tr[[TARGET]])                  # only the classes that are in the training rows
  k     <- nlevels(tr[[TARGET]])
  terms <- keep_terms(RHS_FINAL, tr)
  f     <- reformulate(terms, TARGET)
  re    <- paste0("(1 | ", GROUP, ")")                      # a random intercept per group
  X     <- function(d) model.matrix(reformulate(terms), d)[, -1, drop = FALSE]    # the numbers for lasso / ridge
  tree_vars <- unique(unlist(lapply(terms, function(t) all.vars(parse(text = t)[[1]]))))   # a tree does not use "a:b" or "I(x^2)"
  set.seed(SEED)

  fit <- NULL
  if (k >= 2 && model != "baseline") {
    fit <- tryCatch(switch(model,
      logit = if (k == 2) glm(f, family = binomial, data = tr) else nnet::multinom(f, data = tr, trace = FALSE),
      lasso = glmnet::cv.glmnet(X(tr), tr[[TARGET]], family = if (k == 2) "binomial" else "multinomial", alpha = 1),
      ridge = glmnet::cv.glmnet(X(tr), tr[[TARGET]], family = if (k == 2) "binomial" else "multinomial", alpha = 0),
      tree  = rpart::rpart(reformulate(tree_vars, TARGET), data = tr, method = "class"),
      glmm  = lme4::glmer(reformulate(c(terms, re), TARGET), family = binomial, data = tr)),
      error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(fit)) n_fallback <<- n_fallback + 1          # it could not be fitted: the baseline is used
  }
  if (is.null(fit)) {
    model <- "baseline"
    fit   <- table(tr[[TARGET]]) / nrow(tr)                  # the share of every class
  }
  list(model = model, fit = fit, terms = terms, classes = levels(tr[[TARGET]]), k = k)
}

# the probability of every class (a table with one column per class). A class that is not in the training rows gets a very small probability.
predict_model <- function(obj, te) {
  fit <- obj$fit; cl <- obj$classes
  P <- switch(obj$model,
    baseline = matrix(rep(as.numeric(fit), each = nrow(te)), nrow = nrow(te)),
    logit    = if (obj$k == 2) { p <- predict(fit, te, type = "response"); cbind(1 - p, p) } else predict(fit, te, type = "probs"),
    lasso    = ,
    ridge    = { x <- model.matrix(reformulate(obj$terms), te)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
                 if (obj$k == 2) { p <- as.numeric(predict(fit, x, s = "lambda.min", type = "response")); cbind(1 - p, p) }
                 else predict(fit, x, s = "lambda.min", type = "response")[, , 1] },
    tree     = predict(fit, te, type = "prob"),
    glmm     = { p <- as.numeric(predict(fit, te, type = "response", allow.new.levels = TRUE)); cbind(1 - p, p) })
  P <- matrix(as.numeric(P), nrow = nrow(te))
  colnames(P) <- cl
  full <- matrix(1e-6, nrow(te), length(CLASSES), dimnames = list(NULL, CLASSES))
  full[, cl] <- P
  full / rowSums(full)
}

# fill the missing values with the TRAIN numbers, fit on train, predict test
fit_predict <- function(model, train, test) {
  d <- fill_missing(train, test)
  predict_model(fit_model(model, d$train), d$test)
}

# the predicted class: the most probable one (two classes: positive if its probability is larger than THRESHOLD)
to_class <- function(P) {
  if (BINARY) {
    neg <- setdiff(CLASSES, POSITIVE)
    factor(ifelse(P[, POSITIVE] > THRESHOLD, POSITIVE, neg), levels = CLASSES)
  } else {
    factor(CLASSES[max.col(P, ties.method = "first")], levels = CLASSES)
  }
}
```

### B-8-2. Fit all the models on all of `raw` and look at them

```{r b-fit-all}
fits <- lapply(MODELS, function(m) fit_model(m, dat))
names(fits) <- MODELS
P_all <- lapply(fits, function(o) predict_model(o, dat))        # the probabilities of every model (on all of raw: the models have seen these rows)

# Confusion matrix of every model: the rows are the actual class, the columns the predicted class (a perfect model has numbers only on the diagonal)
conf_long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(MODELS, function(m)
  data.frame(model = m, as.data.frame(table(actual = dat[[TARGET]], predicted = to_class(P_all[[m]]))))))
conf_long$model <- factor(conf_long$model, levels = MODELS)
ggplot(conf_long, aes(x = predicted, y = actual, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile() + geom_text(aes(label = Freq)) + facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(x = "predicted class", y = "actual class", title = "Confusion matrices (all of raw)")
```

```{r b-fit-plots}
if (BINARY) {
  y01 <- as.integer(dat[[TARGET]] == POSITIVE)

  # ROC curve: the closer to the upper left corner, the better; the diagonal = guessing
  roc_long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(MODELS, function(m) {
    r <- pROC::roc(y01, P_all[[m]][, POSITIVE], quiet = TRUE)
    data.frame(model = m, fpr = 1 - r$specificities, tpr = r$sensitivities)
  }))
  ggplot(roc_long, aes(x = fpr, y = tpr, color = model)) +
    geom_line() + geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
    labs(x = "false positive rate", y = "true positive rate", title = "ROC curves (all of raw)")

  # The probability of the positive class for the rows of every actual class: the two groups should be far apart
  prob_long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(MODELS, function(m) data.frame(model = m, actual = dat[[TARGET]], prob = P_all[[m]][, POSITIVE])))
  ggplot(prob_long, aes(x = prob, fill = actual)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 30, position = "identity", alpha = 0.5) + facet_wrap(~ model) +
    labs(x = paste("probability of", POSITIVE), y = "count", title = "Predicted probability by actual class (all of raw)")

  # lasso and ridge: the coefficients (log-odds scale). A lasso coefficient of exactly 0 = the variable is dropped.
  if (fits$lasso$model == "lasso") {
    coefs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("lasso", "ridge"), function(m) {
      cf <- as.matrix(coef(fits[[m]]$fit, s = "lambda.min"))
      data.frame(model = m, term = rownames(cf), coef = cf[, 1])
    }))
    coefs <- coefs[coefs$term != "(Intercept)", ]
    ggplot(coefs, aes(x = term, y = coef)) +
      geom_col() + coord_flip() + facet_wrap(~ model) +
      labs(x = "term", y = "coefficient", title = "lasso and ridge coefficients")
  }

  # mixed model: the random intercept of every group
  if ("glmm" %in% MODELS && fits$glmm$model == "glmm") {
    re_df <- data.frame(group = rownames(lme4::ranef(fits$glmm$fit)[[GROUP]]), effect = lme4::ranef(fits$glmm$fit)[[GROUP]][, 1])
    ggplot(re_df, aes(x = reorder(group, effect), y = effect)) +
      geom_point() + coord_flip() +
      labs(x = GROUP, y = "random intercept", title = "glmm: the effect of every group")
  }
}
```

```{r b-tree-plot}
# The decision tree: the questions it asks, from the top. (A tree made of the root only means: no question helped.)
if (fits$tree$model == "tree") {
  plot(fits$tree$fit, uniform = TRUE, margin = 0.1)
  text(fits$tree$fit, use.n = TRUE, cex = 0.7)
}
```

## B-9. Model comparison: the moving window

The models are compared on rows they **did not see**. With a time column: the model is trained on the last `WINDOW` days, predicts the next `TEST_DAYS` days, and the window moves forward; all the predictions are collected and then scored. Without a time column: K-fold.

The 5 scores (the predicted class is the most probable class; two classes: positive if the probability is larger than `THRESHOLD`):

| score | meaning |
|---|---|
| `Accuracy` | the share of rows with the right class. Larger is better, but a model that always says the big class can look good |
| `BalAcc` | balanced accuracy = the average, over the classes, of the share of the class found. Not fooled by a big class. Larger is better |
| `F1` | two classes: the F1 of the positive class (precision and recall together); several classes: the average over the classes. Larger is better |
| `AUC` | the chance that a row of the class gets a higher probability than a row of another class (several classes: the average over the classes, one against the rest). 0.5 = guessing, 1 = perfect. Larger is better |
| `LogLoss` | punishes a confident wrong probability. Smaller is better |

```{r b-cv-tools}
metrics <- function(y, P) {                                 # y: a factor with the levels CLASSES, P: the probabilities
  pred   <- to_class(P)
  recall <- sapply(CLASSES, function(k) if (any(y == k)) mean(pred[y == k] == k) else NA)         # the share of every class found
  prec   <- sapply(CLASSES, function(k) if (any(pred == k)) mean(y[pred == k] == k) else 0)
  f1_k   <- ifelse(is.na(recall) | (prec + recall) == 0, 0, 2 * prec * recall / (prec + recall))
  auc_k  <- sapply(CLASSES, function(k) if (length(unique(y == k)) < 2) NA else suppressMessages(as.numeric(pROC::auc(as.integer(y == k), P[, k], quiet = TRUE))))
  p_true <- pmax(P[cbind(seq_along(y), match(as.character(y), CLASSES))], 1e-15)                   # the probability given to the TRUE class
  c(Accuracy = mean(pred == y),
    BalAcc   = mean(recall, na.rm = TRUE),
    F1       = if (BINARY) unname(f1_k[POSITIVE]) else mean(f1_k[!is.na(recall)]),
    AUC      = if (BINARY) unname(auc_k[POSITIVE]) else mean(auc_k, na.rm = TRUE),
    LogLoss  = -mean(log(p_true)))
}

# The moving window: for every block of TEST_DAYS days from `from` to `to`, train on the WINDOW days before the block and predict the block
run_sliding <- function(model, data, from, to) {
  ys <- character(0); days <- as.Date(character(0)); Ps <- NULL
  start <- from
  while (start <= to) {
    end   <- min(start + TEST_DAYS - 1, to)
    train <- data[data$.day >= start - WINDOW & data$.day < start, ]
    test  <- data[data$.day >= start & data$.day <= end, ]
    train <- train[!is.na(train[[TARGET]]), ]
    test  <- test[!is.na(test[[TARGET]]), ]
    if (nrow(train) > 0 && nrow(test) > 0) {
      ys   <- c(ys, as.character(test[[TARGET]]))
      days <- c(days, test$.day)
      Ps   <- rbind(Ps, fit_predict(model, train, test))
    }
    start <- end + 1
  }
  list(y = factor(ys, levels = CLASSES), P = Ps, day = days)
}

# Without a time column: K-fold on raw
run_kfold <- function(model) {
  set.seed(SEED)
  fold <- sample(rep(1:FOLDS, length.out = nrow(raw)))
  ys <- character(0); Ps <- NULL
  for (k in 1:FOLDS) {
    test <- raw[fold == k, ]
    ys   <- c(ys, as.character(test[[TARGET]]))
    Ps   <- rbind(Ps, fit_predict(model, raw[fold != k, ], test))
  }
  list(y = factor(ys, levels = CLASSES), P = Ps)
}

run_cv <- function(model) {
  if (HAS_TIME) run_sliding(model, raw, from = min(raw$.day) + WINDOW, to = max(raw$.day)) else run_kfold(model)
}

# a table of the scores, the best LogLoss first
score_table <- function(preds) {
  tab <- t(sapply(preds, function(p) metrics(p$y, p$P)))
  tab[order(tab[, "LogLoss"]), ]
}
```

```{r b-cv-run}
if (HAS_TIME) stopifnot("raw has fewer days than WINDOW: lower WINDOW in the settings" = as.numeric(max(raw$.day) - min(raw$.day)) > WINDOW)
n_fallback <- 0
cv_pred <- list()
for (m in MODELS) { cv_pred[[m]] <- run_cv(m); cat(m, "") }       # (this takes a while: one fit for every model and every block)
cat("\nfits that fell back to the baseline:", n_fallback, "\n")

cv_table <- score_table(cv_pred)
round(cv_table, 3)
```

```{r b-cv-plot}
# the LogLoss of every model (smaller is better)
cv_df <- data.frame(model = rownames(cv_table), LogLoss = cv_table[, "LogLoss"])
ggplot(cv_df, aes(x = reorder(model, LogLoss), y = LogLoss)) +
  geom_col() + labs(x = "model", y = "LogLoss", title = "Moving window: LogLoss of every model")

# the confusion matrix of the best model (the rows are the actual class, the columns the predicted class)
best <- rownames(cv_table)[1]
cat("best model:", best, "\n")
table(actual = cv_pred[[best]]$y, predicted = to_class(cv_pred[[best]]$P))
```

## B-10. The holdout (once)

**Open the holdout only when the analysis above is finished.** Same rule as in section B-9: the models are trained on the last `WINDOW` days before every block of `TEST_DAYS` days of the holdout (the days of the holdout that are already past are used as training days, as in real life). Nothing is chosen with these numbers: they only tell how good the final model really is.

```{r b-holdout}
holdout <- readRDS("holdout.rds")
if (exists("make_class")) holdout[[TARGET]] <- make_class(holdout)       # the example target: the SAME cut-offs as in raw
holdout <- holdout[!is.na(holdout[[TARGET]]), ]
holdout[[TARGET]] <- factor(holdout[[TARGET]], levels = CLASSES)         # the same classes as in raw

n_fallback <- 0
if (HAS_TIME) {
  holdout$.day <- as.Date(holdout[[TIME]])
  full <- rbind(raw, holdout)                                                   # raw followed by holdout
  hold_pred <- lapply(MODELS, function(m) run_sliding(m, full, from = min(holdout$.day), to = max(holdout$.day)))
} else {
  hold_pred <- lapply(MODELS, function(m) list(y = holdout[[TARGET]], P = fit_predict(m, raw, holdout)))   # trained on all of raw
}
names(hold_pred) <- MODELS
cat("fits that fell back to the baseline:", n_fallback, "\n")

hold_table <- score_table(hold_pred)
round(hold_table, 3)
```

```{r b-holdout-plot}
best <- rownames(hold_table)[1]
cat("best model on the holdout:", best, "\n")
table(actual = hold_pred[[best]]$y, predicted = to_class(hold_pred[[best]]$P))        # the confusion matrix of the best model

if (BINARY) {
  # ROC curves of every model on the holdout
  roc_long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(MODELS, function(m) {
    r <- pROC::roc(as.integer(hold_pred[[m]]$y == POSITIVE), hold_pred[[m]]$P[, POSITIVE], quiet = TRUE)
    data.frame(model = m, fpr = 1 - r$specificities, tpr = r$sensitivities)
  }))
  ggplot(roc_long, aes(x = fpr, y = tpr, color = model)) +
    geom_line() + geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
    labs(x = "false positive rate", y = "true positive rate", title = "Holdout: ROC curves")
}

# over time: the daily share of every class, actual and predicted (the best model)
if (HAS_TIME) {
  p <- hold_pred[[best]]
  daily <- rbind(
    data.frame(day = p$day, class = as.character(p$y),         what = "actual"),
    data.frame(day = p$day, class = as.character(to_class(p$P)), what = "predicted"))
  ggplot(daily, aes(x = day, fill = class)) +
    geom_bar(position = "fill") + facet_wrap(~ what, ncol = 1) +
    labs(x = "day", y = "share of the rows", title = paste("Holdout over time:", best))
}
```
